25 An electromagnetic wave has a wavelength of 138 pm in a vacuum.
To which region of the electromagnetic spectrum does this wave belong?
A
radio wave
B
microwave
C
visible light
D
X-ray

hints: Convert $138 \text{ pm}$ to metres using $1 \text{ pm} = 10^{-12} \text{ m}$ and to nanometres to compare with familiar spectrum values.
Recall the order of the spectrum by decreasing wavelength: radio wave, microwave, infrared, visible light around $400$-$700 \text{ nm}$, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray.
Check whether $0.138 \text{ nm}$ is much smaller than visible light and ultraviolet and fits the $10^{-11}$ to $10^{-8} \text{ m}$ X-ray band.
walkthrough: First convert the given wavelength to SI units: $\lambda = 138 \text{ pm} = 138 \times 10^{-12} \text{ m} = 1.38 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m}$, which is $0.138 \text{ nm}$.

Recall typical vacuum wavelengths: radio waves $> 10^{-3} \text{ m}$, microwaves $\sim 10^{-3}$ to $10^{-1} \text{ m}$, visible light $\sim 4 \times 10^{-7}$ to $7 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$, while X-rays are $\sim 10^{-11}$ to $10^{-8} \text{ m}$.
Compare $1.38 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m}$ with these bands: it is about a thousand times shorter than visible light and far shorter than microwaves and radio waves.
A wavelength of order $10^{-10} \text{ m}$ is comparable to atomic spacing and falls squarely in the X-ray region. This is option D

A.explanation: Radio waves have wavelengths of order $1 \text{ mm}$ to $100 \text{ m}$ or more, about $10^{10}$ times larger than $138 \text{ pm}$.

B.explanation: Microwaves have wavelengths of order $1 \text{ mm}$ to $30 \text{ cm}$, far larger than $138 \text{ pm}$.

C.explanation: Visible light has wavelengths around $400$ to $700 \text{ nm}$, about $3000$ times larger than $138 \text{ pm}$.

D.explanation: $138 \text{ pm} = 1.38 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m}$ lies in the $10^{-11}$ to $10^{-8} \text{ m}$ range characteristic of X-rays.
